Title: The Wheat on the Chessboard
Subtitle: An Old Tale from India
Author: by Liz Huyck
Content: Long ago, a wise Indian mathematician called Sessa invented the game of chess to amuse his friend the king. The king was delighted with the game and told Sessa to name anything he liked as his reward, boasting that the wealth of his kingdom was limitless. But instead of gold, jewels, elephants, or palaces, after much thought Sessa told the king that he wished only a few grains of wheat.

“I am a simple man,” replied Sessa, “and my wants are few. But since you enjoy my chessboard so much, give me a `text(single)` grain of wheat for the `text(first)` square, `text(two)` grains for the `text(second)`, `text(four)` for the `text(third)`, and so on. For `text(each square)` `text(double)` the last, as `text(each day)` of play `text(doubles)` our delight. That will mean more to me than all the riches in the world.”
“Very well!” said the king, a little irritated, thinking that Sessa was mocking his wealth. “If that's all he wants,” he told his treasurer, “give it to him!”

The `text(first day)`, the treasurer presented Sessa with a `text(single)` grain of wheat, to the huge amusement of the court. The `text(second day)`, he got `text(two)`, on a little cushion. The great lords roared with laughter. But Sessa kept his thoughts to himself.

On the `text(ninth day)`, Sessa received `256` grains, enough to make a small handful. But the very next `text(day)`, he had `text(two)` handfuls. It took Sessa `text(16 days)` to get enough wheat to fill a large bag. But only `text(one)` more `text(day)` to get `text(two)` bags. The day after, he had `text(four)` bags. The courtiers stopped laughing and started whispering.
By the end of the `text(month)`, wagons filled with grain were rumbling toward Sessa's house, and the treasurer began to look worried. Quaking in his boots, he went to see the king.

“Highness!” he trembled. “Please look over my calculations, but I don't think they are in error. By his simple `text(doubling)`, Sessa has now collected nearly all our stores of wheat! What shall we do? If we continue at this rate the treasury will soon be bankrupt, and I doubt there is enough wheat in the entire world to pay him!”

The king was amazed by the treasurer's words, but he checked and `text(double-checked)` the arithmetic, and there was no doubt. In horror he saw that by the last of the `64` squares, he would owe Sessa a total of `text(18,446,744,073,709,551,615)` grains of wheat! He could not even imagine so many grains — they would make a pile of wheat larger than the largest mountain. That much wheat could not be gathered if all of India grew nothing else for the next `text(2,000 centuries)`!
There was nothing for the king to do but call Sessa before him, confess the foolishness of his rash promise, and take back his boasts about his limitless wealth.
“Sire!” Sessa replied. “Let us say no more about the wheat. I am happy with what I have already — I forgive you the `text(second half)` of the chessboard.”

With that the king and Sessa remained the best of friends and enjoyed many games of chess together. And the clever Sessa got the real reward he had wanted all along — a wiser and more mathematical king.

:box:`ultext(Historical Note)`

Though no one can say for sure if it really happened, this story has been around for as long as chess, which was probably invented in northern India about `text(1,500 years)` ago. It is a fun illustration of how quickly a series of numbers that grows by multiplying can get out of hand, even if it starts out slowly. The amount of wheat for just the `text(first)` square on the `text(second half)` of the chessboard is as much as the entire `text(first half)`!
